title: Nessa and the Moonpetal Dewdrop
markdown:
High in the Frostcap Mountains, where snow gleamed like a million scattered diamonds under the moon, lived a young witch named Nessa. Hair the colour of twilight, a soft dusky shade. Cloak stitched with tiny stars that twinkled merrily whenever she felt a flutter of excitement. Always by her side, or rather flitting just above her head like a guardian shadow, was Gwyneth: a spotty bat, most unusual, fur as dark as midnight, surprisingly large intelligent eyes that seemed to hold the wisdom of a hundred moons. Fiercely loyal. Little heart often thumping like a drum when Nessa was about to embark on something grand, a rhythm only she could truly understand.

Nessa and Gwyneth had a promise to keep, a solemn vow whispered on the breath of a frosty wind. Given to Nessa by the ancient Moonpetal Flower, a bloom of breathtaking beauty that graced the Frostcap Mountains and bloomed only once a century, deep in its hidden heart. In its final radiant moments the flower had gifted Nessa a single shimmering moonlight dewdrop, no bigger than a pea, yet within its tiny orb pulsed the softest purest light, like captured starlight. This dewdrop, Nessa had promised with all her young heart, must be delivered to the oldest most venerable Oak in the Whispering Woods before the moon reached its highest most magical point.

“Are you ready, Gwyneth?” Clear and bright as the mountain air, a hint of adventure. The stars on her cloak gave a tiny excited shimmer.

Gwyneth gave a little squeak of assent, cheerful boldness, velvety wings. “As ready as a dewdrop is for a moonbeam.” They set off, small figures descending from their cozy moss-roofed cottage into the hushed snowy landscape. The cottage door latched with a soft wooden click, and the frost took their footprints at once, as if the mountain preferred not to keep records. Moonlight painted long eerie shadows that danced like playful giants across the frost. Each shadow a silent invitation. Crisp cold air, sharp pine, something ancient and magical that tickled Nessa’s nose. Gwyneth flew a little ahead, then a little behind, checking the dark between the pines the way a careful postman checks a latch.

As they tiptoed through a particularly snowy patch, drifts as soft as clouds, a sudden boisterous gust swept down from the highest wind-scoured peaks. It tugged Nessa’s cloak, little stars jingling like tiny bells, and sent Gwyneth spinning like a tiny spotted acrobat. “Whoa there.” Spots blurring. Nessa, a quick flick of wrist and a whispered incantation, cast a small gentle spell. A puff of warm golden air, a tiny friendly cloud, cushioned the fall, bringing Gwyneth safely back to her shoulder. “You nearly became a snowball. Or perhaps a tiny frozen bat-sicle.” Gwyneth, a little ruffled and indignant, huffed and smoothed sleek fur, a tiny frown on a whiskered face.

They continued. Tall stoic trees giving way to the deeper more mysterious embrace of the Whispering Woods. Moonlight softer, filtered through ancient interwoven branches, dappled on the forest floor. Then a frantic rustling, frustrated grumbles like pebbles tumbled in a tin can.

“Blast and bother. Where did that billowy bluebird go? Always with the wind-borne messages, never a sensible package that stays put.”

Nessa and Gwyneth exchanged a glance. Someone in a pickle. Peeking through frosted ferns, leaves sparkling: a goblin no taller than a mushroom, beard like a tangled clump of green moss, spectacles perpetually slipping down his nose. Sorting a haphazard pile of leaves, twigs, fallen berries, muttering with great consternation. Gribble had a system that looked, to the untrained eye, very much like organised chaos. The goblin postmaster of the Whispering Woods: habit, and perpetual disarray.

“Excuse me.” Soft but clear, a distant bell.

Gribble jumped, spectacles skittering further. “Who’s there? Bartholomew? Did you finally send that apology note to the pixies about the giant mushroom incident?”

“No, it’s Nessa. And this is Gwyneth.”

He peered, large bulbous eyes widening behind askew glasses. “Ah, the young witch. And the spotty flitter-mouse. What can Gribble do on this fine frosty eve? Lost your way to the enchanted mushroom patch?”

“We’re on a special delivery.” Quiet seriousness of the promise. She held up the tiny glowing dewdrop, pulsing pearly in her palm. “To the oldest Oak in the woods.”

Gribble’s darting eyes fixed on it. Mouth, usually a worried frown, creased into a wide hopeful grin, a few missing teeth. “Aha. A special delivery. And it sparkles so. The lost parcel from the Moon Moth’s cousin. The recipe for luminous moon-cakes. I’ve been expecting it for ages.” Before Nessa could protest, surprising speed: he snatched the dewdrop, tucked it into a rough burlap pouch on his belt.

“Hey.” Gwyneth’s spots darkening with alarm. “That’s not for you. That’s for the Oak.”

“It is, it is.” Already hobbling away, clumsy boots squelching. “A very important delivery for me to deliver, of course. Gribble the Postmaster always delivers.”

“Oh dear.” A little exasperated, a hint of amusement. “A complicated promise. A rather unique interpretation of delivery.”

Gwyneth fluttered off, body vibrating with determination. “We’ll get it back. Follow that mossy beard. He can’t outrun the truth, or a determined witch and her bat.”

A rather comical chase through the moonlit woods. Gribble, despite short legs and the weight of his duties, surprisingly quick: darting behind ancient trees with gnarled roots like reaching fingers, scrambling over fallen logs as if they were stepping stones. He vanished once into a thicket of frost-ferns and emerged with a twig in his beard, still clutching the pouch as if it were the last parcel in the world. Nessa and Gwyneth followed, a few well-placed magical nudges, Gwyneth guiding with keen senses, little squeaks like a compass, Nessa’s bursts of speed, star cloak trailing like a comet’s tail. Twice they nearly had him; twice he slipped aside with the practised panic of a goblin who had spent years chasing bluebirds. They could hear him muttering, muffled by trees: “Such a lovely glow. Just the thing to cheer up my collection of particularly shiny pebbles. The envy of all the glow-worms.”

Near a hollow log that seemed to sigh with the wind, they cornered him. Fumbling with the dewdrop, trying to admire its glow, spectacles practically falling off. “Gribble, please. That dewdrop is a gift for the oldest Oak. The last light of the centennial Moonpetal Flower. It needs to be planted at its roots to bring it good fortune.”

He stopped, hands trembling. Looked at the dewdrop, at Nessa’s earnest face, at Gwyneth hovering, large eyes deep with concern. A slow dawning. “The oldest Oak? Centennial Moonpetal? Oh my word. And I thought it was a rare sparkle-berry for my prize-winning gnome garden. I was so looking forward to showing it to the hedgehogs.”

He sighed, wind through dry autumn leaves. “My apologies. My mind is always in a whirl, like a startled squirrel. I do try my best, but sometimes the messages get tangled, like roots in a storm.” He handed the dewdrop back, large fingers surprisingly gentle. “The oldest Oak. Just beyond that mossy hill, where the shadows sing and the fireflies dance like fallen stars.”

Nessa smiled, warm and forgiving. “Thank you. And thank you for trying to deliver it, even if it was the wrong delivery.”

Gwyneth landed on Nessa’s shoulder, nudging her cheek. “He really does try.” Spots a calming dappled pattern.

With Gribble pointing the way, they hurried on. Air still and reverent, woods holding their breath. There, bathed in the purest most ethereal moonlight, an Oak so grand, so ancient, it seemed to touch the sky. Branches like welcoming gentle arms, moss and silver lichen. A guardian, silent and magnificent.

Nessa approached with profound respect and placed the moonlight dewdrop at its gnarled ancient roots. For a breath nothing happened, only the tick of frost and Gwyneth’s small heartbeat against her collar. Then it pulsed with brilliant light, a soft warm glow spreading upwards, illuminating bark and sleeping leaves. A deep resonant hum, pure contentment and ancient wisdom, a lullaby sung by the earth. The lichen took the light as if it had been waiting a hundred years and did not intend to hurry the last minute.

“We did it.” Quiet triumph. The promise kept.

Gwyneth chirped, nuzzling her ear. They stood a long moment, watching the Oak, scent of damp earth, ancient wood, lingering Moonpetal. No one named the lesson. The Frostcap Mountains stretched silent and majestic, holding their own weather. The moon began its slow graceful descent, rose and lavender. Gribble, if he sorted any more parcels that night, might still mix moon-cakes with oaks. The dewdrop stayed at the roots, which was how you knew a postmaster could snatch a promise and still point the way home.
characters: Nessa (young witch of the Frostcap Mountains), Gwyneth (a loyal spotty bat)
